Alright I have the following project I need to complete. It's vague, but my teacher gave me the following instructions: 

<pasted_content id="8936">
roject 2: Claude Code and agentic development
In this project, we will explore:
Project level 1:  Gather data on how students are permitted (or encouraged) to use genAI for CS courses around the country.  How are other CS departments talking about AI/genAI in their official publications.  Do they have a positive take on AI?  Do they discuss collaboration with AI.  How are software engineering courses handling AI around the country.  Make a dashboard to visually communicate the findings.  Identify an approach to analyze this data.  
Do this using: 1. Agentic development* with Claude Code.  This involves working with Claude to write specification files and run tests for the project as a whole, and individual phases of the project.  In this mode, you may be only minimally looking at code directly.  More of your interactions will be around developing the plans, specifications, and reviewing the validations. 
Spec driven development- These specifications should allow you to routinely clear or compact the context window (You: Prepare to clear.  Claude:  (preps). You: /clear).  These specifications should enable you to inspect Claude's code evaluation (#2 below), create the document of your contributions (#3 below) and document token usage (#4 below). 
Outside of this goal, make visual interfaces using web technologies (or other UI/visual tools): 
2. Validating the code and reporting validation results.  When you work with Claude, it runs many tests automatically.  These tests may be hard to keep track of and look at yourself.  For this project, explore an alternative way to view and inspect and communicate the tests.  Suggestion: a web interface to display and explore (search, filter....) the tests it is running.  Validation report must include evidence for correctness, show the tests and results, and help a skeptical reviewer accept the validity of your code.  This could include your direct review of code, but be sure to document your reviewing steps with Claude. 
3. Documenting and describing your contribution to the project and Claude's contribution to the project.  Here you ensure that Claude records progress, with timestamps.  Stores your questions and its responses.  You will make with Claude a web-based interface to document your project timeline, your contributions, etc. 
4. Documenting your token usage and how different practices (clear, compact) or project steps (gathering data, processing data, writing code, running validations) impact token usage.  Make a web-based interface for token usage. 
Finally: 
Evaluating the project for how well it meets the initial goals.  This step will be completed primarily by you, not Claude. But you can use Claude to get you information you need for this evaluation. 
You will complete this project following an agentic development approach- the code will be primarily written by an AI agent (Claude Code), with you directly supervising.  You will do less direct code editing than in an AI assisted development workflow.   Your job is to make sure 1. the agent is producing accurate, efficient and valid code and 2. your code meets the objectives of the project (the goals, addresses user needs).  
Use Claude Code, pro-level ($20/month).  I suggest the Opus 5.5 model.  I was able to complete my previous project without running out of tokens, and Opus 5.5 
Please publish your project and all documentation results on github and on the web.  
Reflect: How do you feel about an agentic development approach vs an AI assisted development approach (if you have a basis for comparison). 
 
Deadline:
Nov 10- application
Nov 11- documentation
Nov 12- presentation
 
 

* Def:
* Manual coding- you write code. Maybe occasional search/AI help with library, what function will do X
* AI assisted- You are looking at the code, and asking for help from AI for parts of the code, but you make decisions for every code addition, change etc.
* Agentic – An agent writes the code. You may only minimally review code, but primarily look at requirements, specs, tests etc.
</pasted_content id="8936">

---

**Coaching**

Two things about how you prompted this one.

First, you did something genuinely right and it is worth naming so you repeat it: "when you say something works PROVE IT" is the highest-leverage instruction in your message. It is why this turn opened with six commands against your actual filesystem instead of a confident essay about what Claude Code "generally" stores. Without that line I would likely have planned around a logging system you did not need to build. Keep using it, and consider making it stronger: "prove it or say you have not checked" closes the gap where I quietly assert the unverifiable.

Second, the thing to improve: you gave me a 600-word assignment and asked for "all the potential options and tradeoffs" with no boundary on what you had already decided. That invites me to re-ask things you may have settled weeks ago. A sentence like "I have already decided X and Y, do not relitigate those" would have bought you a shorter, sharper first turn. Non-technical is not the same as having no constraints, and your constraints are the most useful thing you can hand me.

**Claude Code feature for this task:** project-level `CLAUDE.md`. Your global one at `~\.claude\CLAUDE.md` is injected into every turn of every project, and right now it is spending that budget on canon-keeper's MCP SDK pinning rules while we work on a policy study. A `CLAUDE.md` inside this project's folder gets loaded alongside the global one and is the correct home for this project's rules, which also lets the canon-keeper block move out of your global file and into canon-keeper's own. Phase 0 sets that up, and the immediate payoff is that every single turn from then on carries instructions that actually apply.

## Done this turn, with proof

- **GitHub works.** `gh auth status` reports you logged in as `Marcus-Hollimon`. Your repo `Project-2-AI-Use-In-Schools` exists, is public, and is empty.
- **Git identity is set.** It now reports `user.name = Marcus` and `user.email = [email removed]`. The failure in your screenshot was my fault: I gave you bash syntax (`&&`), and your terminal is Windows PowerShell 5.1, which rejects it. About the email: your GitHub profile already shows it publicly, so committing with it exposes nothing new.
- **Global CLAUDE.md is rewritten.** It went from 95 lines to 70. A line-by-line comparison shows only what I meant to change: the canon-keeper section is gone, the header is updated, and three rules are added (PowerShell-safe commands, high-level explanations first, tell you when you're misusing me). Everything else is word-for-word the same. A byte-identical backup is at `~/.claude/backups/CLAUDE.md.2026-11-08.before-canon-keeper-removal`.

## I audited what I told you last turn, and several claims were wrong

| What I said | Verdict | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Transcripts record tokens, timestamps, prompts and tool calls for every turn | Holds | |
| `/compact` is recorded | Holds | 25 flagged rows, all `true` |
| Biggest session: 4.50B cache reads vs 13.9M output | **Wrong, about 2x too high** | Each reply is saved as several rows, and each row repeats the same token counts. That session has 12,131 rows but only 5,733 real replies. Corrected: 2.18B vs 5.51M |
| Session files can simply be added together | **Wrong** | 316 replies appear in two or more files, because reopening a session copies its history into a new file |
| The 04:51 / 04:52 gap was a `/clear` | **Wrong** | 1,362 of the new file's 1,364 rows were copied from the old one, so that was a reopened session. How `/clear` shows up in the data is still unknown |
| Hooks can record `/clear` exactly | **Unverified** | I had only seen two other hook types working |
| Weight tokens by billed rates | **Wrong for you** | You pay a flat Pro fee. What you actually spend is a percentage of your usage limits |
| CLAUDE.md was "90% canon-keeper" | Exaggerated | 38 of 95 lines, so 40% |

The main conclusion survives and gets stronger: cache reads outweigh output 395 to 1 after the fix, not 324 to 1.

This is good news for deliverable 2. My first analysis double-counted tokens and misread a reopened session, and a deliberate check caught both. A skeptical reviewer wants exactly that story. I'll keep these audit scripts and their output as the first tests in Phase 1, so your validation report opens with a real error that got caught instead of a wall of green checkmarks.

## Two findings that change the plan

**1. Your real budget, read straight from your account.** You're on Pro. You've used 50% of your weekly limit, and it resets **Tuesday Nov 10 at 1:00 AM EST**. Your 5-hour window is at 12%. Extra usage is turned off, so hitting the limit means a hard stop until the reset. The timing is mixed:
- Bad: today and Monday, when the heaviest work (the research) happens, only have half a week of budget left.
- Good: you get a full fresh week starting the night before the application is due.

Your standing rule says never cut investigation to save tokens. I'm keeping that rule. The way to honor it on this budget is to cut the number of schools, not the quality of the work on each one.

**2. Canon-keeper is still wired into this folder outside CLAUDE.md.** `C:\Claude Folder\.claude\settings.json` runs canon-keeper's code checks and tests after every file write or edit, with a 3-minute timeout. It hasn't fired yet only because I've been writing files through the shell. Once Phase 0 starts editing files the normal way, it would run a retired project's test suite on every single edit. I haven't checked whether it also fires in sessions started inside a subfolder. Your OK last turn covered CLAUDE.md only, so I left it alone. I'd remove it and keep a backup.

## My opinion on the plan

**On your four answers:**

1. **Stratified ~40 schools.** Right design, but the number shouldn't be fixed before we measure.
   - Pilot 5 schools first, one per institution type.
   - Read how much of your weekly limit each school costs, then choose the final number. If one school costs 2%, then 40 schools cost 80%, which isn't possible before the reset.
   - With about 8 schools per group, comparisons between groups are descriptive, not statistically significant. Say that plainly in the write-up.
   - Save the actual web page behind every coded claim (your own "read real bytes" rule, applied to websites), so a reviewer can check any data point against its source.
2. **I write the UI, you review.** Right for this assignment. Since you aren't reading code, "review" should mean clicking through the live site against a checklist written into each spec. That checklist with your pass/fail marks becomes documented evidence of your contribution.
3. **React.** Keep it. My static-site recommendation was more cautious than this situation needs. The search-and-filter views for deliverable 2 are easier to build well in React, and React comes with tools for testing the UI, which strengthens deliverable 2. The real risk is publishing it to the web, and Phase 0 deals with that first.
4. **Protect the study.** Agreed, with one hard truth: the study is also the phase most likely to run out your budget. The pilot is what actually protects it.

**What I'd change in my own plan from last turn:**
- **Deliverable 4 needs a deliberate experiment, not just old data.** To show how clear and compact affect usage, this project's own sessions need to contain clears and compacts at known moments, labeled by phase. So at every phase boundary I'll record a usage reading, you'll do a deliberate `/clear` or `/compact`, and the state file will log both. The first `/clear` also serves as the test of how `/clear` really appears in the data, replacing my wrong guess.
- **Never publish raw transcripts.** This folder's history includes 73 calls to a company-search tool from other work, plus your email and pasted materials. Only derived numbers, and prompts from this project that you've reviewed, should go public.

**Timeline:**

| When | Budget | Work |
|---|---|---|
| Sun Nov 8 | remaining 50% | Phase 0, Phase 1, codebook, 5-school pilot |
| Mon Nov 9 | rest of that 50% | Main collection (size set by the pilot), your 10 hand-coded schools |
| Tue Nov 10 | fresh week from 1 AM | Interfaces and validation; application due |
| Wed Nov 11 | | Documentation, your evaluation |
| Thu Nov 12 | | Presentation |

**On "I haven't decided anything":** that means last turn's coaching point, telling me what you'd already decided, rested on a wrong assumption. Drop it. It also means the four answers you clicked were your first real decisions, which is why I reviewed each one above instead of treating them as settled.

---

**Coaching**

1. **"Dwell on what has been done so far" was the most valuable thing you said this session.** It produced the audit, and the audit found four wrong claims. Notice what actually caused it, though: not the switch to a "smarter model," but your instruction to re-check earlier work. A model switch doesn't make old claims any more or less true. Ask for an audit of earlier claims at every phase boundary, whichever model is running.
2. **Say your whole intent, not just the first place it applies.** "Fix the CLAUDE.md, I will never do canon-keeper stuff" really meant "remove canon-keeper from my setup everywhere." Because you named only the CLAUDE.md, the hook had to wait for a second approval. Stating the broader goal would have let me finish the cleanup this turn.

**Claude Code feature for this task:** the app's usage card. It shows the same 5-hour and weekly percentages I read for you above. Check it at the start and end of every phase. Those readings are the most honest data you can get for deliverable 4, because on Pro the limit is what you're really spending, not dollars.

entries.text:
Phase 0 is done, and your site is live at **https://marcus-hollimon.github.io/Project-2-AI-Use-In-Schools/**

## What's proven, and how

| Claim | Proof |
|---|---|
| The code works | Lint is clean, the build is clean, and 17/17 tests pass. Every run is saved in `validation/runs/`. |
| The tests aren't decorative | I broke the app twice on purpose. Breaking tab clicks failed exactly the click test. Breaking page addresses failed 10 tests. After restoring, both files were byte-identical and 17/17 passed again. |
| Publishing works | GitHub's own machine ran lint, tests, and build before each deploy. Both runs passed (27 s and 18 s). |
| The live site is the current code | The live page's footer shows commit `58801b4`, which is the latest on GitHub. That proves pushing to GitHub rebuilds the site automatically. |
| Every page survives a fresh load | Tested in a real browser: each page loaded fresh (confirmed by an in-page marker getting wiped), showed the right heading and tab, and produced zero console errors. |
| Nothing from memory | Configs came from the exact versions in use (Vite 8.3.6, Vitest 5.1.0). The workflow's five security-pinned action versions match Vite's own doc character for character. |

Budget: Phase 0 cost about **1 point of your weekly limit** (51% to 52%) and 10 points of the 5-hour window. You have roughly 48% of the week left before Tuesday 1 AM.

## What went wrong along the way

- **The shell tool silently ate backslashes** in three lines of code. The linter caught it before anything ran, and I rewrote those lines so they contain no backslashes at all. It's now a rule in the project's CLAUDE.md.
- **My first browser check proved less than it looked like it did.** Switching between `#` addresses doesn't load a fresh page, and my first marker test only covered one page. My own checks flagged both problems, and the table in `validation/manual-checks.md` is from the corrected run. Both failures are recorded there too, because a reviewer should see them.
- **Copying Vite's deploy file word for word gave CI a different Node version** than your machine (26 vs 24). It's now pinned to 24, and the second deploy confirms CI used Node 24.
- **Not proven: the reload key itself.** My browser pane ignores F5. A fresh load is technically the same thing as a refresh, but the actual keystroke is your check.

## Your turn: the Phase 0 checklist

Open the live site in **your own normal browser** (not my pane, which ignores reload keys) and check:
1. The site loads.
2. Clicking each of the four numbered tabs shows its own title.
3. On **Token usage**, press **Ctrl+F5**. You should still be on Token usage.
4. The commit code in the footer (`58801b4`) matches the latest commit on your GitHub repo page.
5. On GitHub, you can find the `specs/`, `progress/`, and `validation/` folders.

Tell me how it went and I'll record your result, with a timestamp, as your review in `validation/manual-checks.md`. Then type `/clear`, and in the fresh conversation type: **"Read progress/STATE.md and start Phase 1."** That `/clear` does two jobs at once: it's the context reset between phases, and it's the controlled experiment that shows how `/clear` really appears in the transcript data. Last time I guessed at that and got it wrong.

---

**Coaching**

1. **"Start Phase 0" was two words, and that was enough.** It worked because the spec carried the detail: what to build, what "done" means, how it gets checked. That is the core idea of spec-driven development, and it's what lets you `/clear` safely. Keep going-ahead prompts short only when a written spec exists. When none exists, a two-word prompt hands every decision to me.
2. **Don't skip the checklist to save time.** The assignment grades your supervision, and right now the repo honestly says "Marcus's checklist: not done." If you approve Phase 1 without doing it, the project's claim that you reviewed Phase 0 has no evidence behind it. Five minutes of clicking is the cheapest proof of your contribution you'll get all project.

**Claude Code feature for this task:** `/clear`, combined with the `progress/STATE.md` file. After a clear I remember nothing, so the next session's quality depends entirely on what that file says. That makes your `/clear` a live test of whether this project's specs actually work, which is exactly what your teacher asked you to demonstrate. If the next session picks up Phase 1 correctly from one sentence, that's your evidence.

Yes, we'll use `/compact`. One hard limit first: **I can't compact myself.** I have no tool that runs `/compact`; only you can type it. The only automatic version kicks in at 97% of my 1M-token context, which would be very late and expensive. Every turn re-reads the whole context, so a bloated context drains your weekly budget faster. So here's how it'll work: at good stopping points I'll update `STATE.md`, commit, take a usage reading, and give you the exact line to paste. That's now a rule in the project's CLAUDE.md.

**Recorded:** your 5/5 checklist pass is in `validation/manual-checks.md` with its time, and all ten boxes in the Phase 0 spec are ticked. It's committed and pushed as `2e6ce59`. Your decision to use compact instead of clear is logged in `progress/decisions.md`.

**Now is a good point.** Phase 0 is finished, everything is committed, and I took a "just before /compact" reading: weekly 53%, 5-hour 28%, context 293,955 tokens. Paste this:

```

Keep: the project lives in C:\Claude Folder\Project-2-AI-Use-In-Schools; progress/STATE.md and specs/ are the source of truth; token figures must be deduplicated by response id; never publish raw transcripts; the shell tool collapses double backslashes; Marcus prefers /compact and I must take a usage reading right after one. Next: write specs/phase-1-instrumentation.md.

After it finishes, say "continue". My first step will be the "after /compact" usage reading, so the compact's effect gets measured.

**Hard truth about compact-only.** Deliverable 4 asks how *both* clear and compact affect token usage. If we never `/clear`, you can only describe compact; you can't compare the two. One deliberate `/clear` at a safe point, say after Phase 1 once `STATE.md` has proven itself, would give you that comparison. It's your call, and if you'd rather skip it, the write-up should say plainly that the comparison wasn't run.

---

**Coaching**

1. **Stating a preference ("I prefer compacts") was exactly right.** It changed the workflow in one sentence. What would have made it stronger is one clause of reasoning, like "because I lose too much with clear." That tells me whether to protect the comparison or drop it, instead of asking you a follow-up question.
2. **"Can you compact yourself?" was a good question to ask rather than assume.** The answer is no, and if I'd silently agreed to do it, Phase 1 would have started with a bloated context and nobody noticing. Keep asking "can you actually do X?" whenever a plan depends on my abilities.

**Claude Code feature for this task:** `/compact` with focus text, which is the line above. A bare `/compact` lets the summarizer decide what matters. Focus text tells it what must survive, and you've used that form 7 times before. The specific rules that are easy to lose (dedup, privacy, the backslash quirk) are exactly the things a generic summary drops.

I've written the Phase 1 plan ([specs/phase-1-instrumentation.md](specs/phase-1-instrumentation.md)). Phase 1 builds a script that turns our Claude Code history into the data for tabs 3 and 4 (Contributions and Token usage). Before writing the plan, I measured how your compact shows up in the history files, so the plan is built on facts rather than guesses.

**What the compact showed (measured, saved in [evidence/phase1-recon/](evidence/phase1-recon/recon-output.txt)):**
- **The compact worked as hoped.** Context went from 305,065 tokens to 14,969 of conversation, in 56 seconds. The app now shows 81,551 tokens in total.
- **Most of what's left is fixed overhead.** About 78,000 of those 81,551 tokens are the same every turn: tool descriptions, connectors and system instructions, re-sent each time no matter what we talk about.
- **The compact's own cost is not in the history.** The history files record every normal step, but the step that writes the summary leaves no trace. Only the app's usage percentages see it. The Token usage tab will say so openly instead of quietly under-counting.
